	‘Grey’s Anatomy’ Boss Unpacks Season 23 Premiere and Teases Dolly Parton Episode, Texas Spinoff and Whether This Really Could Be the Final Season
	



			
			
	
						

									Courtesy of Disney
	
					


							
		

	SPOILER ALERT: This interview contains major spoilers from “Collide,” the Season 23 premiere of ABC’s “Grey’s Anatomy,” streaming on Hulu.

	There’s a new sheriff in town at Grey Sloan Memorial Hospital.

	In the Season 23 premiere of “Grey’s Anatomy,” the doctors of TV’s most indomitable hospital are convened for the grand opening of a lavish new VIP floor. Ostensibly designed to give wealthy patients a luxury stay — complete with private suites, high-level security, hotel-quality bedding and access to private chefs — the venture is backed by Seth Norton (James Wolk), a physician-turned-businessman who also happens to be Grey Sloan’s new chief of surgery.

	Following the simultaneous departures of former chiefs Owen Hunt (Kevin McKidd) and Teddy Altman (Kim Raver) at the end of last season, long-time fans might have expected another familiar face to take the helm. Instead, showrunner Meg Marinis opted for a corporate outsider, using Norton’s appointment to reflect the stark financial sacrifices modern hospitals must make just to keep their doors open to the general public.



	

					James Wolk 
									Courtesy of Disney
	



	“I was really interested in this idea of a VIP floor and exploring the upstairs-downstairs of medicine, which is really being talked about lately. The healthcare disparity is only growing more, unfortunately, and it’s something that felt very topical,” Marinis tells Variety. “We at Grey Sloan have always provided VIP care to the entire hospital, but I wanted to see what that conflict would look like for our doctors.”


	Meredith (Ellen Pompeo), naturally, is the first doctor to express her skepticism about the VIP initiative and the man who will now be running the hospital where she began her career as an intern. “Meredith says at the end of the premiere, ‘This will implode,’ so I think everybody should be waiting to see if it implodes,” Marinis says with a laugh. “We’ll see [Norton] in conflict with a bunch of our series regulars. He was brought in for a purpose. Medicine’s business for him, and that’s not typically how our doctors have treated their careers.”

	In the wide-ranging conversation below, Marinis breaks down all of the personal and professional twists from the premiere; addresses the perennial chatter that this season of “Grey’s” could be the show’s last amid another wave of industry-wide budget cuts — and offers a status update on the untitled West Texas “Grey’s” spinoff, which she is co-creating with Shonda Rhimes.




	

					Debbie Allen
									Courtesy of Disney
	



	
		Meredith makes it immediately clear to Seth, Catherine (Debbie Allen) and Richard (James Pickens Jr.) that she feels like the hospital is already prioritizing corporate interests over the hospital’s standard of care. “Grey’s” has explored that friction in the American healthcare system before, but what new sides of that conversation are you looking to open up this season?	

	I think it’s different, because Meredith is now not just a resident, she’s an attending who also has an ownership stake in the hospital. The risk of a hospital shutting down and patients losing all their doctors, all their care — that is something you have to really balance. We will explore what it looks like when a hospital shuts down, too. It’s not going to necessarily be Grey Sloan, but you’ve seen it happen in L.A., and sometimes it can happen without a moment’s notice. It’s something I’ve always been interested in. And also, who’s going to take all those patients?


	
		How much will we see of Ellen as Meredith this season? Will she still appear in around seven episodes like she has in past seasons?	

	We haven’t confirmed that yet, but I say this every year: I want her as much as we can get her. When she’s here on the show, it’s great for us. She’s got a couple of different projects happening on the side, so at this point it just becomes a scheduling game. We love Meredith; we’ll have Meredith in as many episodes as we can. We just have to respect her other projects too.


	
		You have previously told me about how you tend to stretch Meredith’s arc across multiple episodes, so that Ellen can come in and shoot a bunch of scenes at once to accommodate her busy schedule. Did Ellen feel particularly strongly about where she wants Meredith to go this season?	

	100%. We talk about the creative ahead of time. I want her to feel like she has a part in the stories that we’re going to tell for Meredith. She’s played the character for 23 years. She’ll often have little things that she wants to talk about, but sometimes, she’ll see something in the news or she’ll read about something in medicine, and she’ll call me and say, “Are y’all thinking about doing this?” She’s definitely a collaborative partner, and we try to make it work. It just depends, again, on schedule.


	
		Is Meredith’s arc going to be tied to this new patient (Martin Martinez) who is in the foster care system and potentially has cancer?	

	They will have more stories together. That’s not her only arc, but yes.
	
		Scott Speedman has already wrapped production on Season 2 of “R.J. Decker,” so he will presumably be available to return to “Grey’s” this season. Will we get to see Meredith and Nick’s wedding onscreen this season?	

	I’m going to see him soon! That’s what I’ll say.


	
		Bailey (Chandra Wilson) realizes that she needs to take something off her plate in order to take on this new challenge of getting her masters in public health, so she decides to name Winston (Anthony Hill) the new residency director. How much will we see of Bailey in the classroom this season?	

	We’ll see a little bit of her at school, but it was important to me that we still see her in the hospital, because what she’s seeing in the hospital is inspiring her educational journey. But we’ll see her on campus in Episode 2.


	
		What are you looking to explore with Winston and Jules’ (Adelaide Kane) relationship this season, now that you have the added complication of Winston being directly responsible for the residency program?	

	Well, I’m exploring some mess! Because we’ve created a big old mess for them. Twenty-three years ago, this storyline would’ve been much different, but now we’re in 2026. This has been their fear for as far back as when they started experiencing this attraction — that they can’t be together. There’s a power dynamic. Honestly, maybe they were thinking about coming clean to everybody, but then he couldn’t say no to Bailey because being residency director is also good for his career. So I think they’re both flawed, right? They’re not making every decision the way they should, so I think that we’re going to see that rocky path.



	

					Caterina Scorsonne, Jen Landon
									Courtesy of Disney
	




	
		At the end of last season, Toni (Jen Landon) was finally ready to take a leap and pursue a romantic relationship with Amelia (Caterina Scorsone) — until she caught her hooking up with Cass (Sophia Bush). Toni was so hurt that she felt the need to leave the state to get away from Amelia temporarily, but the two finally reconcile and share a steamy kiss in the premiere. What did you want to convey through the writing of that speech, and what’s next for them?	

	If you look at the history of the character of Amelia, even going all the way back to “Private Practice,” she has this tendency to self-sabotage, and I was really interested in seeing a piece of growth from that self-sabotage where she can at least acknowledge and name it. She didn’t intend to cheat on Toni with Cass because she wanted to cheat. She slept with her because she was hurt, and she thought that Toni was going back to her ex-wife. We made it look like Toni was going back with the ex-wife.

	We have debates about this in the writers’ room on who was at fault here, because a lot of people are like, “Team Amelia! Toni strung her along in those last two episodes saying, ‘I might go back with her. I might not go back with her.’” But then a lot of people are like, “No, Amelia slept with somebody else! She’s dead to Toni!” So it really depends on who you ask, but I think those two actors have fantastic chemistry. I love working with Jen. I love the character of Toni and what she does also for Ben Warren. That’s a really fun dynamic to watch. We’re going to see more of that as well. So we’re just going to have to see if they can find this new happiness, but it’s “Grey’s.” We’ll throw things at them, don’t worry.


	
		Are you planning to delve more at all into Toni’s background before Grey Sloan? Will we meet Toni’s elusive ex-wife this season?	

	Never say never!


	
		Besides her personal relationship with Toni, will Amelia be dealing with anything new on the professional side this season?	

	Yes. This will affect all the doctors, but for her, there’ll be more of a story because some of our residents are going to have to choose what area they’re focusing on. We know that there’s a familial connection to neurosurgery, so we’ll definitely explore that between her and Lucas [Niko Terho].



	

					Jen Landon, Chris Carmack, Camilla Luddington 
									Courtesy of Disney
	




	
		Jo (Camilla Luddington) is still dealing with the trauma of almost dying while giving birth to her and Link’s (Chris Carmack) twins midway through last season. She officially quits her job by the end of the premiere. This feels particularly like a fork-in-the-road moment for her — and it’s not entirely clear if she’ll be able to go back to her old self after this experience.	

	We’re not going to wrap it up in Episode 2. We have a lot of people quit and then come back. But her traumatic health scare really impacted her last season. PTSD after birth trauma is something that affects so many women, and I didn’t want to gloss over the fact that it takes time to process. So we’ll see her question that, and it’s going to affect how she chooses to parent her kids. She’s a fighter. This is going to be a time of personal discovery of a couple of ups and downs. The really difficult part is she thinks that she’s the only problem at home right now, but there’s a whole other thing brewing that she doesn’t know about.


	
		You pointed out to me last season that Link is a little bit more traditional, in the sense that he doesn’t always want to ask for help. You also mentioned that your writers’ room will explore addiction “in a more nuanced way than the stereotypical thing of seeing someone popping pills every five minutes.” What are those more nuanced conversations about drug dependency going to look like going forward?	

	We’re going to see him get a little bit deeper into what’s going on, and then we’ll explore those conversations. Right now, he’s in denial, right? There are stages of addiction that impact everyone. It’s a different journey for everybody, but we’re really interested in telling the story of how someone is functioning in all areas of their life, but then there’s this little secret going on. It makes it even more heartbreaking because everybody else thought everything was fine at home and at work. He will hide it at first, and then it makes it much more painful, but it will come out.


	
		“Grey’s” being “Grey’s,” Simone (Alexis Floyd) discovers that she is pregnant with either Lucas or Wes’ (Trevor Jackson) baby. Why did you want to throw yet another baby into the middle of a love triangle on this show?	

	It’s going to take a few episodes to unravel, and that’s why we told the fertility story last season. We had been planning it that way. It’s different in the sense that she just found out that she may not be able to have children the old-fashioned way, so that adds another layer to it. She’s definitely not ready to have a baby, but she doesn’t know if this is the one time that she’s got. I think a lot of women have to struggle with that. Do you put everything on pause? Do you have it? Or do you make the decision to focus on your career? And is she going to go through that alone, or is she going to tell one of these guys?


	
		Did Alexis always know that you were planning for Simone to get pregnant, or did you also spring this reveal on her when she read the premiere?	

	I waited to tell her until the premiere. Honestly, we planned it last season, then I wrote the premiere and didn’t do it because everyone on social media thought we were going there, and then I missed it and I put it back. So I’m as transparent a showrunner as I can be to the cast, but I didn’t want her to be stewing over that over the summer if I wasn’t sure.



	

					Harry Shum Jr. 
									Courtesy of Disney
	




	
		Richard fired Blue (Harry Shum Jr.) at the end of last season for injecting a patient with an unapproved drug, and Blue has been keeping himself occupied by taking online French lessons. He ends up treating his teacher secretly at Grey Sloan after he realizes that she is suffering a medical emergency, and he is clearly still itching to get back to practicing medicine. What else has he been up to since his firing, and what is next for him?	

	For Blue, there’s been a lot of video-game playing and sitting on the couch, and he’s going through the different stages where he is in shock and denial. He’s trying to pretend that he’s fine and filling up his day with activities like French lessons, but that isn’t how it is in Episode 2. He’s saying that he’s happy being unemployed, but there’s no way that character is happy not practicing medicine. We’ll have to see whether or not he is going to sacrifice and go into something else, or if he’s not going to give up and try to get back into Richard’s good graces. Also, it’s not necessarily Richard who will let him back. Maybe there’s another way into it…


	
		How much will we see of Harry Shum Jr. this season now that he’s busy competing on “Dancing With the Stars”?	

	I’ve got to give Harry Shum Jr. so much credit. I know he’s doing “Dancing With the Stars” because I was approached about it and he is on my TV, and I don’t have him on Tuesdays. But besides that, everything is completely normal, except when you see him practicing with Jenna Johnson outside of the stages. He must not be sleeping, because he’s not called me once to say, “I need time.”
	
		So have you been holding “DWTS” viewing parties every week with the cast and crew?	

	Yes. We put up the East Coast feed on a screen outside the stages with a QR code reminding people to vote, and a few of us have gone to the tapings.


	
		Looking ahead to the next couple of episodes, I understand that Episode 3 features a Dolly Parton impersonator as a patient.	

	We were in the middle of shooting that storyline when Dolly Parton passed. It was a story that was pitched out of our writers’ room by the writer of Episode 3, Jase Miles-Perez. We were laughing, and we thought it was a hilarious storyline and so endearing because, again, who doesn’t like Dolly Parton? The impersonator storyline is so fun, but it was emotional over here, in particular for Debbie [Allen]. She was directing that storyline when we had to walk over there and pull her aside and tell her what happened. Obviously, it wasn’t planned, but we were able to honor her with the storyline, and it must have been a trip. I don’t understand how Debbie did that. We were literally filming the storyline that day on stage — and the title of that episode [“It’s All Wrong, but It’s All Right”] is a Dolly Parton song.


	
		Are the rest of the characters going to pick up the slack in trauma now that Owen and Teddy are gone?	

	Yeah, right now, that’s how it’s going. I really didn’t want to say that those two characters or doctors at the hospital were replaceable. So I think even just having somebody like Seth Norton as chief, that’s showing how much this hospital will miss Teddy.


	
		Are there any plans right now to revisit Maggie (Kelly McCreary)? She appeared in the 450th episode last season, and shared with Meredith and Amelia that she is pregnant via a sperm donor.	

	That’s so funny. Kelly texted me yesterday. She was letting me know about a play or something that she was doing. I would love to have an update on Maggie. It depends on where we are creatively. She probably has a baby by now, unless it’s the longest pregnancy like Jo Wilson’s was.


	
		Are you able to confirm how many episodes you are making for Season 23?	

	No, that hasn’t been confirmed with me yet.
	
		You and I have spoken about the challenges of trying to make “Grey’s” — which features one of the largest ensembles on TV — in today’s financial climate. You’ve had to reduce the number of episodes that characters appear in, and like so many other shows, you’re potentially facing a reduced episode count for this season.	

	Every show is feeling it. You even feel it when you’re developing a new show, when you learn what’s available. I’ve had conversations that I never had before when starting up the new [“Grey’s” spinoff]. Every episode at Season 23 is a gift, and a lot of people here feel that way. Maybe it’ll go on to Season 50, but probably not. You look at the budget every episode, and you’re like, “Can I go on location? Can I not go on location? Can I afford visual effects? Can we not see a green screen?” Every episode, there are conversations like that.

	No one’s told me that the end is coming, so for that I’m grateful. I feel like because of what this show has done, they will give me a little bit of a heads’ up. But it’s always top of mind because of what you’re seeing in the industry. We always know that this year could be the [final] year, but so far, we’re still going; they’re still allowing us to make these episodes. And if there is a shorter order or not, again, we’re just grateful that we’ve had what we’ve had, and we’ll take whatever we can get. It’s an honor to tell these stories.


	
		What is the status of the “Grey’s” West Texas spinoff that you are co-creating with Shonda?	

	It’s in the works, and we’re very, very excited about it. It’s so cool to get the opportunity to create something with her, especially about something that is so dear to me. I can’t say much about it because I’m not authorized to do it, but it’s still everything that you’ve heard or read. It’s in rural West Texas. It is a spinoff, so we’ll connect it to “Grey’s.” The timing on that is still being discussed, just because we want to do what’s best for both shows. All those conversations are happening literally as we speak, and I wish I could clone myself.


	
		You were born and raised in Houston, Texas. Did you pitch Shonda the idea of a West Texas spinoff and have her come on board to co-write the pilot with you? How involved is she in this new expansion of the universe she created?	

	She’s very involved. She’s been involved from the very beginning. She wanted to expand the universe, and I wanted to be involved in it. I’m from Texas, so I’ve always wanted to tell a story about West Texas. I’m a huge fan of the TV shows that have been in West Texas. My father’s from there, and I’ve spent quite a bit of time there.

	Something that I’ve always been interested in just from working on “Grey’s” is what’s happening in these medical deserts, and the amount and how quickly these places are closing. People are having to travel an hour just to get a sore throat looked at. The amount of birthing centers that have closed — people have to travel two hours to have their baby. And it’s happening not just in West Texas; it’s happening all over the country. I think Vermont is a state that has one of the worst medical deserts. So even though it’s in Texas, I think it will apply and resonate with what’s happening in all small towns in America.

	This interview has been edited and condensed.

title: Why Did Netflix Boot Bela Bajaria?
description: Fear and loathing are running high as Hollywood processes Thursday’s shock firing of Bela Bajaria from her post as Netflix chief content officer.Yes
body:
Fear and loathing are running high as Hollywood processes Thursday’s shock firing of Bela Bajaria from her post as Netflix chief content officer.Yes, the company that popularized the “Keeper Test” is known for abrupt exits. But despite Netflix’s recent stock struggles, many considered Bajaria too big to fail.Word of her ouster leaked before the executive had the chance to address most of her internal teams — an announcement dovetailed with news of her incoming replacement, the venerated film and TV executive Peter Rice. As the former general entertainment chairman of the Walt Disney Company, Rice’s bona fides are clear — “I wish I bought stock this morning,” one huge talent rep said about Netflix’s new hire — but it doesn’t explain how Bajaria fell out of favor so fast.One word that came up in nearly a dozen conversations with industry players this afternoon about Bajaria’s pink-slipping: “scapegoat.”Netflix is obviously against the ropes again, after slowing user engagement on the service rattled Wall Street investors and layoffs came this week as a sacrifice to the share price. But Bajaria’s dismissal makes it clear, according to the numerous sources we spoke with, that content is once again going to take it on the chin.“People always blame the content,” said the source, “but you don’t lay off 1,000 people unless there’s a big problem with the business model.”Bajaria’s exit echoes similarly shocking removals in Netflix history — notably that of Cindy Holland, the company’s first content queen who oversaw flagship hits like “House of Cards,” “Stranger Things” and “The Crown.” Holland was ousted in 2020, when Sarandos combined English-language and international content under Bajaria (elevating the latter to the largest autonomous content job in the streamer’s history).Holland, one insider with knowledge of Netflix observed to Variety, built a business of boutique hits. Bajaria’s foresight was sharper, investing in local language productions and building up Netflix’s global presence (almost two dozen international offices were opened during Bajaria’s reign). She is also credited internally with pushing the streamer into live entertainment. Bajaria was on the “ground floor” of licensing deals with WWE and the NFL, which have proven significant draws for the ad-supported tier of Netflix subscribers, per the source. Her talent relations were on par with others at her level (Bajaria was ubiquitous at premieres and launches in film and TV, most recently at Sarandos’ side at the L.A. premiere of Ben Affleck’s “Animals”).“The problem isn’t engagement,” said yet another person with knowledge of Netflix. “It’s that the only lever to pull for revenue growth is raising the subscriber price. How’s that Bela’s problem? Where’s the CFO and the CEO?”Interestingly, we hear that Rice came into play only a few weeks ago when he was reported to be interviewing with Skydance co-CEO Ynon Kreiz for a top position at that newly combined company. The lunch meeting, one source familiar with the men said, was called so Kreiz could request that Rice replace him on the board of his former company Mattel. Regardless, it alerted the town that Rice was done with semi-retirement (a producing deal with A24) and ready to come back to a big job. Another hot Thursday rumor said that Rice also met recently with NBCUniversal about a post there. One source familiar with NBCU said there was no job in play for Rice under Donna Langley’s expansive umbrella, so it’s unclear what he would’ve met about. A spokesperson for NBCUniversal had no comment.Another lunch may have proven consequential in Bajaria’s exit. Earlier this year, Netflix co-CEO Ted Sarandos was spotted breaking bread with HBO chief content officer Casey Bloys. Was Sarandos courting Bloys for a top job at the streamer, perhaps to take the job then held by Bajaria? Soon, the spin machine reframed the meeting as a friendly gathering, floating the idea that it was a pitch for Bloys to sign a production deal under Bajaria if he did not want to find a way to work at the merged Paramount-Warner Bros. At a Bloomberg conference last week, Sarandos downplayed the meeting: “He’s a good guy,” he said about Bloys. “For some reason, we had a very well-publicized lunch.”Perhaps. But in hindsight, now that Sarandos has leveled the ax on Bajaria after 10 years, is a lunch ever really just a meal? Rice’s recent focus has been as the head of ceremonies and content for the Los Angeles 2028 Olympic Games — but now Rice focuses on a more urgent task. The exec has been on the open market in the years since he was let go at Disney. He’s seen as the rare exec who has spent time heading up both major film and TV businesses, so the job of chief content officer at Netflix, where he’ll oversee both, makes sense. He’s also well-liked and respected from his time at 20th Century Fox, heading up Fox Searchlight and later the Fox network, and eventually becoming president of parent company 21st Century Fox prior to Disney’s acquisition.“Surprise” was also a common refrain both inside and out of Netflix on Thursday about the turn of events. But a few hints had already been out there: Netflix is set to report its Q3 earnings next Tuesday, so such a move would have to be made beforehand. And with co-CEOs Sarandos and Greg Peters not going anywhere, the sacrificial lamb next in line was Bajaria. Observers speculated that the Q3 results are likely to be extremely disappointing for the streamer, which is already facing some tough headwinds.At that same Screentime event, anyone reading between the lines might have guessed that Sarandos was getting antsy with Netflix’s current low-growth status. In particular, he was asked about Netflix’s slower growth (2% year-over-year growth in user engagement during the first half in 2026). “Yes, overall, we’re not growing as fast as I want us to, and we’re working on making that move faster,” he said. Turns out Bajaria’s exit was a part of that change. Now all eyes turn to Rice’s plans for Netflix, and whether those plans will include some of Bajaria’s lieutenants, such as U.S./Canada head of scripted series Jinny Howe and film lead Dan Lin.Bajaria may also have hit thin ice with Sarandos after the streamer won just 16 Primetime Emmy Awards this year — its worst showing since 2016 and down from 30 in 2025. That’s quite a turn from 2021, when it tied the record for most Emmys won by an outlet in a single year, with 44.Along with the Emmy slump, Netflix hasn’t premiered a culture-defining hit in the vein of “Stranger Things” in quite some time. But it’s still fielded some of the most-watched programs of the year, including “His & Hers” and Season 4 of “Bridgerton.” Bajaria is known for her keen creative eye, honed over the years at places like CBS and NBCUniversal (where she was ultimately head of Universal TV before moving to Netflix in 2016).“In her decade at Netflix, Bela’s impact has been undeniable — from attracting new talent, bringing live sports, concerts and events to driving the company’s global expansion and push into new areas of entertainment,” WME co-chair Richard Weitz tells Variety. “Her relationships with talent have been integral in Netflix’s relationships with A talent across the platform. Simply put, she’s been transformational and I know her worldwide team and the talent who have worked with her will miss her.”Rice will not inherit a bus of happy campers. He’ll have to galvanize a team that lost a slew of executives Wednesday as a result of pink slips. On the TV side, that included Carolina Garcia, who has been let go as director of original series after a decade with the streamer, as well as scheduling head Andy Kubitz, Lisa Lang McMullen (director, overall deals, series), Andrew McQuinn (director, original series), James Oh (director, original drama series) and Jason Pan (manager, original series creative development).

	The remaining film group appears safe for now, as Lin’s team saw a major sacrifice in VP Doug Belgrad earlier this week. Morale will need tweaking, budgets adjusting and a slew of new lunches will be scheduled. What you can count on, per one of the streaming insiders, is that “eventually, everyone’s time comes at Netflix.”

body:
The Singapore Media Festival will add a dedicated creator economy event to its lineup this year, launching the Asia Creator Summit alongside the long-running Asia TV Forum & Market when its next edition takes place Dec. 1–5.

	The festival is hosted by Singapore’s Infocomm Media Development Authority (IMDA). The new summit (ACS) and ATF will form the two main strands of this year’s event, which carries the theme “The Heart of the World’s Stories.”
	

	“New technologies and audience behaviors are constantly reshaping how we consume, distribute, and monetize content today,” said Yvonne Tang, assistant chief executive of IMDA’s Media Industry Group. “Our latest SMF 2026 program is designed to help Singapore’s media professionals and companies adapt in this evolving media landscape, by strengthening their creative and commercial capabilities through wide ranging partnerships and business opportunities.”


	ACS will run Dec. 4–5 at Marina Bay Sands under the banner “Create. Monetize. Scale.” The two-day program will feature more than 20 sessions, mixing keynotes, panels and master classes with practical sessions. They are aimed at turning creator output into lasting businesses and IP that can travel. Generation Experience (GenXP) curated the summit with Monica Khan, founder and CEO of Creator Revolution.

	Speakers include South Korean creator Kimpro, who counts more than 130 million subscribers and a career total of 154 billion views. Japanese creator Issei, whose dialogue-free comedy has drawn audiences worldwide, has upward of 75 million YouTube subscribers. Also on the bill is AJ Eckstein, founder and CEO of U.S. company Creator Match, which has helped brands including Anthropic, Fiverr, Notion, Lovable and Zapier set up and grow their creator programs.
	

	Singapore-based executives on the lineup include GRVTY Media CEO and co-founder Johnathan Chua, DU Media Holdings CEO Kelvin Tan and Gushcloud International group CEO and co-founder Althea Lim.

	Creators will also get a shot at brand work. Mandarin Oriental, Singapore is running a Creator Pitch Challenge tied to its 40th anniversary, while Bloomr.SG’s “Creator Lab” will hand out up to SGD100,000 ($78,000) in awards for creator-focused ideas. Calls for proposals open in early November.

	“Creators are playing an increasingly influential role in how audiences discover, engage and connect with content, brands and ideas,” said Michelle Lim, founder and CEO of GenXP. “We are excited to launch Asia Creator Summit as part of the Singapore Media Festival, creating a platform for creators and the wider industry to learn from one another, share experiences and shape what comes next.”

	ATF, organized by RX Global, will return to Marina Bay Sands Dec. 1–4 for its 27th edition. Organizers expect more than 5,000 content players from Asia and further afield, representing 60 countries and regions.

	“The Attention Economy” is the theme of the opening-day ATF Leaders’ Dialogue. Executives from East West Bank, Omdia, TikTok, Unilever, Webtoon Productions and YouTube will examine how fandom and shifting viewing habits are changing content distribution, financing and branded entertainment. They will also look at how companies can extract commercial value from audience engagement.

	A new strand, “The AI Era | Entertainment Reimagined,” will combine a dedicated program with a zone focused on what AI means for content creation, IP rights and regulation, and on how creative work can be safeguarded. Huace Group, Moonmax and Studio Meta K will take part, as will the Motion Picture Association, the Television Academy and the World Intellectual Property Organization. ATF will also host the final round of AI Hackathon 2026, backed by Yoywow Space and Visify, which will include a live creative contest and screenings of chosen entries.

	Canada and Indonesia will each bring a new pavilion to the market. Microdrama will be a bigger focus at this year’s edition, and ATF will keep its drama showcases running alongside accelerator and pitching programs that pair producers of new IP with development partners.
	

	“ATF has evolved beyond a marketplace to become a premier industry platform for strategic commercial announcements, content launches, and thought leadership from some of the entertainment industry’s most influential voices,” said Yeow Hui Leng, managing director, Singapore, of RX Global. “Emerging technology, including AI, will be a key part of this conversation, alongside critical issues such as regulation, financing, distribution, monetization, and content innovation.”

title: Nawazuddin Siddiqui to Star as Delhi Street Detective in ‘Kabootar’ (EXCLUSIVE)
description: Indian thespian Nawazuddin Siddiqui is attached to lead “Kabootar,” the debut feature from writer-director Ishan Sharma, produced by Nikhil Chaudha
body:
Indian thespian Nawazuddin Siddiqui is attached to lead “Kabootar,” the debut feature from writer-director Ishan Sharma, produced by Nikhil Chaudhary of MDC Filmworks. 

	The film is structured as a co-production between MDC Filmworks in India, Haiku Films in France, and Rein Film in Norway, with Rohit Saxena serving as co-producer on the Indian side. Principal photography is scheduled to begin in Delhi in early 2027.


	Set against the crumbling architecture of Old Delhi, “Kabootar” centers on Mehboob, a street detective who secretly reads letters written to a Djinn in search of prospective clients. His path crosses with Naoko, a Japanese tourist carrying the weight of a painful past, and Ruby, a young child searching for his parents.
	

	Siddiqui is among the most decorated actors of his generation in Indian cinema. He has appeared in Anurag Kashyap’s “Gangs of Wasseypur,” Ritesh Batra’s “The Lunchbox,” and Nandita Das’s “Manto” – all of which debuted in Cannes – and starred in Netflix’s hit thriller series “Sacred Games.” He received an International Emmy nomination for his lead role in Netflix film “Serious Men.”

	Chaudhary said: “Nawaz is an actor of extraordinary range. He can be dangerous in ‘Gangs of Wasseypur’ and heartbreakingly gentle in ‘The Lunchbox.’ He’s also one of the few Indian actors with a real international presence. His films have gone to Cannes multiple times, and he has been nominated for an International Emmy. For an India-France-Norway co-production, that matters enormously in taking ‘Kabootar’ to audiences around the world. Just as important, he knows Delhi intimately. For Ishan and I, this film is a love letter to the city, and we needed an actor who could understand it, feel it and embody it. He does all three.”
	

	Sharma, who developed the script through the production and storytelling Workshop at the Festival des 3 Continents in Nantes – formerly known as the Produire au Sud Workshop – added: “Nawaz has been an invisible collaborator to a generation of young writers and directors, myself included. We write with his performances in our minds. From ‘Anwar Ka Ajab Kissa’ to ‘The Lunchbox,’ I’ve always admired the intensity and love he brings to a character, and his rare ability to move between hope and despair, light and dark, without losing either. ‘Kabootar’ asks something of him that audiences haven’t seen before. To have him take that leap with us is a gift. I can’t wait to build this world with him.”

	The project has been selected for a series of international market showcases, including the Tasveer Film Market in Seattle, Film Bazaar in Goa – organized by India’s National Film Development Corporation (NFDC) – and the NFDC lineup at this year’s European Film Market in Berlin. Later this month, Chaudhary will pitch the film in the APN+ Track of the Asian Producers Network in Singapore.

	Casting director Dilip Shankar, whose credits include “Life of Pi” and “Monsoon Wedding,” said: “Nawazuddin will bring Mehboob’s eccentric humor, emotional depth and quiet vulnerability to life with rare authenticity. The character demands mischief, rage, tenderness and grace. With his rooted presence and remarkable nuance, Nawazuddin embodies Mehboob’s essential contradictions. His performance anchors ‘Kabootar’ in the lived-in, poignant texture of Old Delhi.”

	Sharma is a graduate of the Satyajit Ray Film & Television Institute. His short films “The God of Panic Street” (2019) and “A Season of Mangoes” (2022) have played international festivals and collected several awards, including the Cinema Experimenta Award.

	MDC Filmworks has previously produced five films, among them Sanjoy Nag’s “Yours Truly,” which premiered at the Busan International Film Festival, and Rajat Kapoor’s dark comedy “Kadakh,” which premiered at the Tallinn Black Nights Film Festival, where it won best screenplay. Haiku Films, founded by Thomas Jaeger, Antoine Delahousse, and Claire Trinquet, produced “Fi” (Grand Prize, San Sebastián 2022) and co-produced “Treasure” (Berlinale 2024). Rein Film, founded by Mathis Ståle Mathisen and Aleksander Olai Korsnes, is known for “My Fathers’ Daughter” (Toronto 2024).
	

	Key crew includes cinematographer Udit Khurana (“Bayaan,” “Ghaath”), sound designer Sethu Venugopal (“Mother,” “Nocturnal Burger”), and casting director Shankar.

	“Kabootar” was curated by CineV, Nina Lath Gupta’s platform connecting projects with financiers and investors.

title: ‘Norm: The Tale of Norm Macdonald’ Review: Judd Apatow’s Juicy and Haunting Portrait of a Comedy Star as Troubled as He Was Hilarious
description: Stand-up comedians have always had a reverence for what they like to call a “comic’s comic” — a fellow comedian who works with such distilled purit
body:
Stand-up comedians have always had a reverence for what they like to call a “comic’s comic” — a fellow comedian who works with such distilled purity and edge, diving head-first into the gnarly metaphysics of comedy, that the comics end up worshipping him more than the public does. (He’s the stand-up-comedy equivalent of an ultimate cool indie-rock cult band.) Gilbert Gottfried was a comic’s comic. So are Larry David and Doug Stanhope and Maria Bamford. And Norm Macdonald was one too, except that as you watch Judd Apatow’s juicy and haunting documentary “Norm: The Tale of Norm Macdonald,” you realize that there was a special thing about him. He was a comic’s comic…who everyone else loved too.
	

	As the movie demonstrates, Macdonald’s credentials as a comic’s comic were unassailable. We see his very first network television appearance on May 9, 1990, on “Late Night with David Letterman,” where he did a bit about the devil commanding someone to kill his family and chop them into bits and stuff the pieces into a duffel bag. (Then the killer learns that the devil is a friend who was kidding.) He speaks in that familiar halting deadpan; he already knows how to draw the audience into his head.


	On “Saturday Night Live,” where Macdonald, starting in 1993, spent four seasons as one of the all-time great hosts of Weekend Update, he returned, over and over, with a bluntly obsessive fixation that couldn’t be denied, to the subject of O.J. Simpson, and to the fact that Simpson had murdered his wife. Why was this funny? Because every time Macdonald made a joke of it, his assertion of O.J.’s guilt was a way of tapping back into the shocking unreality of it. His every O.J. joke had the effect of a giddy slap. He would not relent, and that wound up getting him fired from “Saturday Night Live” (Don Ohlmeyer, the president of NBC’s West Coast division who was responsible for axing Macdonald, was O.J. Simpson’s best friend). Now that’s a comic’s comic thing to do.
	

	On “SNL,” and in his legendary litany of late-night talk-show appearances, and in his stand-up routines, Norm Macdonald had an oxymoronic quality — a slightly disconnected aggression, where he would zero in on a topic, and a joke, that he knew would be prickly, and that might take him “over the line,” but he couldn’t help himself. He had to say the naughty thing, to blurt out the forbidden. Telling that joke would be a catharsis; it would be comedy. Not telling it would be defeat.

	At times, he had a streak of Andy Kaufman’s antisocial hostility, as if comedy was his way of testing both himself and the audience, seeing what they would accept, and seeing if they would accept him. A strange thing that emerges in “Norm: The Tale of Norm Macdonald” is that Macdonald was a compulsive liar, in both his stand-up act and his life, the two planes of existence sometimes entwined around the same deception. That’s part of why he always seemed a bit of a space cadet. You could never really tell whether he meant what he was saying. We learn that he never went to high school…and also that he did (and graduated when he was 14)…that he never went to college…but actually did as well. On the eve of the pandemic, he described himself to an audience as “a young 68” (he was 60 at the time). He also describes himself, to Larry King, as “deeply closeted,” and when King asks if that means he’s coming out as gay, he says no, he’s straight…and then indicates that claiming to be straight is an expression of how closeted he is. You can hear Andy Kaufman chortling in his theater-of-the-absurd heaven.

	Yet the thing about Norm Macdonald is that he executed all this with a smiling charm and a winsome agreeability that made him irresistible to a wide swath of fans. He wasn’t a prickly punk — more like a transgressive Teddy bear. In the early days, including the “SNL” years that made him famous, he was quite handsome, with a lean face and twinkly eyes and dimples and a coif of curly hair and a killer grin that made him look like the slightly goofy cousin of Paul Newman. Fifteen years before Norm Macdonald, Chevy Chase had been the first break-out superstar of “Saturday Night Live,” transforming his own Weekend Update quizzicality into big-screen celebrity, and he accomplished this not because he was a great actor but because he had a sublime detachment coupled with tall preppie good looks that he used ironically. His handsomeness was part of the joke, as well as the cushion for it.
	

	Macdonald, though, didn’t use his looks in that way; they just kind of existed alongside the bratty edge of his comedy. And so when he was booted from “SNL,” he acted like he’d been kicked off a cliff. He was still out there in the culture, but he floundered around, and this, as the documentary captures, was related to his strange and slippery personality: his compulsive sincerity (which meant that he didn’t quite know how to package himself), his compulsive put-ons (which meant that he was actually scared to show who he was), his compulsive insecurity (which meant that he didn’t truly believe in himself as a star), mixed with an element of self-sabotage (his way of confirming all those anxieties about himself).

	After all of that, “Norm: The Tale of Norm Macdonald” is rooted in what a beloved comedian Norm MacDonald was, and still is. In the opening montage, several people, like Howard Stern, reference the rabbit hole you can get into just by going onto YouTube and watching clips of Macdonald on late-night talk shows. He had countless appearances that were gems, because he always invested his talk-show time with a spark of danger. He couldn’t just be a straight shooter, but he had to make his put-ons feel real. At times, he was as philosophical as Lenny Bruce — but Bruce talked about religion only to mock it, whereas Macdonald, at one point, reveals that he’s a Christian who’s a true believer. (This is a man who would introduce his sidekick as someone who jerked off punks for $15 under a bridge.) It’s all part of his mystery.

	The movie is spanked along by clips of Letterman, Jerry Seinfeld, Conan O’Brien, and Dave Chappelle, and Apatow, working with the editor Jake Hostetter, assembles the comedy snippets in an entrancing way, so that we feel the underground sprawl of Macdonald’s career. He could be a great impressionist (his Bob Dole on “SNL” may have helped turn the 1996 presidential election; his Quentin Tarantino was inspired). He kept doing stand-up, but didn’t require the comedy stage to be great; just talking to Jane Fonda on his video podcast, “Norm Macdonald Live,” he was insanely funny. We see his appearance change quite a bit over the years, as he evolves into a puffier version of himself, something that happened in part because he spent his last nine years secretly fighting leukemia. (He died in 2021.) Yet the audience stayed with him — at least, more than the entertainment industry did.
	

	Macdonald wasn’t the first “incorrect” comedian to run afoul of the comedy police, but it felt like he was the first such comic of a certain day and age (namely, ours). He should have had his own late-night talk show, but when he learned that he was up for one — and that he had been passed over for the yuppie dullard Craig Kilborn — that was a sign that his comedy was ruffling feathers. At the same time, he cultivated incorrectness in a way that could be mindless. When he went on “The View” and said that Bill Clinton was guilty of “murder,” he claimed that he was just doing a bit, but since the “bit” fed into right-wing conspiracy theory, it seemed like an episode of sour derangement. And when he defended Roseanne Barr, after her racist tweet in 2018, he did it out of loyalty (one of his first gigs was as a writer for “Roseanne”) but in a tone-deaf way, as if what she’d said in her tweet was some trivial joke. (It was not; it was egregious.) All of this fed into the perfect shitstorm that was The Decline of Norm Macdonald.

	We pretend that comedy is just fun, a means to an end — the end being to make you laugh. But the few who are chosen to be “comic’s comics” occupy that rarefied stratosphere because they know that comedy is more than laughter, and that laughter is more than we give it credit for. You laugh for a lot of reasons, but one of those reasons can be when an idea goes off in your head like a small explosion. That’s why comedy can tickle your soul, snap you back to life, cleanse you. And that’s the kind of comedian Norm Macdonald was. He had a devilish gleam, but he provoked a laughter that sparked you and lifted you up, landing you on the side of the angels.

title: Busan Takeaways: Record Crowds Meet a Political Storm as Asia’s Producers Close Ranks
description: The Busan International Film Festival drew its largest film audience in more than a decade at its 31st edition, which ran Oct. 6–15, while a politi
body:
The Busan International Film Festival drew its largest film audience in more than a decade at its 31st edition, which ran Oct. 6–15, while a political firestorm over a Korean box office hit and an Iranian director’s war speech kept politics in the spotlight.

	These are Variety’s takeaways from the festival and its Asian Contents & Film Market (ACFM).

	Audiences Turn Out, Market Holds Steady


	Screenings drew 200,043 admissions, the festival’s highest tally since 2015. Counting talks, outdoor events and side programs, total attendance reached 277,027, around 40,000 more than the milestone 30th edition last year. Organizers pointed to a new opening date and a bigger screening slate.
	

	Community BIFF, the audience-programmed strand in Nampo-dong, pulled in 29,511 visitors, more than 1.7 times last year’s figure. BIFF Everywhere took films to a record 18 locations, among them Buddhist temples, traditional markets and a National Assembly building in Seoul.

	The ACFM, which ran Oct. 10–13 at BEXCO under the theme “Core and Expansion,” counted 30,484 visitors, up 1.6%. Registrations climbed 4.3% to 3,158 participants from 1,266 companies in 58 countries. Exhibitors rose 17% to 339 companies, 49 of them first-timers, and Czech & Slovak and Cambodian pavilions made their debuts.

	“The biggest obstacle is funding,” ACFM director Ellen Y.D. Kim told Variety. “The scale and the role of the market have grown quickly, but public support has not kept pace. National funding for ACFM has stayed at the same level for two years running.”
	

	“For anyone who wants to work with Asia, there is no place as efficient over four days,” she said.

	Korbinian Haeutle, project manager for Europe! Hub, which ran a stand with EFP and Unifrance, said the quality of the market was very good. “The meetings are good and it feels like many new distribution companies are coming up. Everyone is quite happy,” he said.

	Malaysian filmmakers Woo Ming Jin, director with Greenlight Pictures, and Lau Kok Rui, director and screenwriter with Thousand Sales Pictures, said BIFF brings everybody from Asia together, “so for us it’s a very important festival.”

	“You can count on everyone being here, exchanging about policy changes, sharing project updates… It’s good to see what people are doing. It’s motivational,” they said.

	Politics Takes the Stage

	The festival’s opening week was shadowed by “The Assassin(s),” Hur Jin-ho’s thriller about the Aug. 15, 1974 shooting of first lady Yuk Young-soo, wife of then-President Park Chung-hee. The film opened Sept. 23 and topped the Korean admissions chart, but conservative politicians and online critics accused it of distorting history.

	On Oct. 1, BIFF called off “Actors House: Lee Min-ho,” a career conversation with one of the film’s stars. A day later, production company Hive Media Corp. withdrew the cast and crew from all of their festival appearances, including the opening ceremony and an outdoor stage greeting, citing the safety of audiences and attendees. The move came after a conservative group announced daily protests outside the home of lead actor Yoo Hae-jin.

	The row reached the competition jury’s press conference the day after the opening ceremony, where a reporter raised the question of historical fact and creative freedom. “Specifically regarding the film you mentioned, I have not seen it, though I have noticed there are some controversies. It depends on each individual’s feelings,” jury president Zhang Yimou said. “Creation and historical truth: what does historical truth really mean? History is also written by people, so is history itself truly real? Sometimes that in itself is a question mark.”

	“But as creators, we respect every creator’s vision,” he added.

	Fellow juror July Jung, the director of “Next Sohee” and “Dora,” said: “What I feel now, even though it isn’t my film, is that my heart feels so cold as a filmmaker.”
	

	Later in the festival, around 20 filmmakers, among them directors Chung Ji-young and Lee Myung-se, held a press conference in Busan urging politicians to stop using the film as a political weapon and to leave its judgment to audiences. They also criticized the main opposition People Power Party, whose 109 lawmakers had written to the Singapore International Film Festival asking it to withdraw the film. Singapore has kept “The Assassin(s)” as its Oct. 21 opening title.

	Politics returned at the closing ceremony. Majidi’s “Midday Meal,” the story of a rural schoolteacher, won the Busan Award for best film from Zhang’s jury. After Zhang handed him the trophy, Majidi spoke against the war in Iran, focusing on a U.S. military strike in February on a school in Minab that killed 156 civilians, 120 of them schoolchildren. He dedicated the award to the people of Iran.

	“They will stand firm to the end and fight to get their independence back,” Majidi said.

	“I wish for a future with no war,” he added.

	A-List Status, Star Wattage

	This was Busan’s first edition since FIAPF recognized it as an A-list festival, and the second year of its competition, which featured 13 Asian titles. The win means “Midday Meal” can go straight to the Oscars’ international feature race without a national selection.

	Eddie Cahyono’s Indonesian drama “Ibuku” took the special jury prize, and Lee Yun Chan won best director for Taiwan’s “To Be Ordinary.” Best actor was shared by Zhou Xun for Gu You’s “The First Taste of Loneliness” and Himeno Kashun for “Satoko Always.” Li Danfeng, sound director on “The First Taste of Loneliness,” received the artistic contribution award. Zhang’s jury also included Bi Gan, July Jung, Moon Choi, Samal Yeslyamova, Ishikawa Kei and Tran Thi Bich Ngoc.

	The guest list matched the new status. Michelle Yeoh, back on the Busan red carpet after a 15-year absence, was named Asian Filmmaker of the Year at an opening ceremony hosted by Kim Minha, where Ann Hui received the Camellia Award. Former festival chair Kim Dong-ho was honored with the Korean Cinema Award. Fan Bingbing and Charlotte Gainsbourg also walked the opening night carpet, along with Alfonso Cuarón, making his first official trip to Korea.
	

	Isabelle Huppert brought “All About Corinne,” Maggie Gyllenhaal visited Korea for the first time and Koreeda Hirokazu presented “Look Back.” Lee Chang-dong arrived with his Netflix drama “Possible Love” and its cast, Jeon Do-yeon, Sul Kyung-gu, Zo In-sung and Cho Yeo-jeong. Na Hong-Jin, Kim Jeewoon, Im Kwon-taek, Lee Myung-se, Bae Chang-ho, Fukada Koji, Lav Diaz, Rintaro, Reza Rahadian and Christine Hakim were also in town, as were Zhou Xun, Hyun Bin, Jung Woo-sung, Son Suk-ku, Hwang Jung-min, Kim Hye-ja and Japan’s Michieda Shunsuke.

	Fan, Kim Jeewoon and cinematographer Hong Kyung-pyo curated Carte Blanche selections, while Actors’ House sessions featured Kim Go-eun, Kim Minha, Ryu Seung-ryong, Shin Min-a and Ju Ji-hoon. Gainsbourg, Gyllenhaal, Cuarón, Na, Diaz and Rintaro led master classes and talks.

	Producers Close Ranks, Money Gets Creative

	At Producer Hub, the Producers Guild of Korea (PGK) and Indonesian producers’ association APROFI formed the Asian Producers Alliance, with producer bodies from the Philippines, Taiwan and Hong Kong also signing on. The founders see it as the seed of a standing coalition of Asian producers working together on co-productions and policy. PGK also signed cooperation agreements with Italy’s CNA and the Sakha Filmmakers’ Union.

	“Co-production used to be an option; now it is an essential strategy for sharing risk,” market chief Kim said.

	New capital was on the table as well. Korean content investor Solaire Partners and Japanese entertainment financier Questry signed a memorandum of understanding on Oct. 12 to set up a Korea–Japan content fund worth KRW100 billion ($74.6 million). The market’s new Investor Summit gathered 20 companies, including Korean investor-distributors, venture capital firms and investors from Indonesia, Singapore, the U.S. and France, for a closed-door roundtable. Cinema by Brand, launched with Innocean and PGK and sponsored by Hanwha, paired three film projects with brand backing.

	Financing individual films remains hard. Hollywood executives at a panel featuring UTA, Gold House, Lionsgate and HYBE  saw an opening for Asian talent and stories rooted in specific cultures, while conceding that getting projects funded is still a struggle.

	Kevin Law, market consultant at Film Export U.K. and a sales agent, said Busan is a steady market for keeping relationships and building partnerships. “I think one thing that’s obvious this year is that it’s difficult for independent films,” he said.
	

	Li-yan Fan, international sales representative at France’s Ecce Films, made her first trip to Busan looking for co-production partners. “Co-production is becoming inevitable, but it still depends on the nature of each project and the resources available where you’re shooting,” Fan told Variety.

	AI Gets Down to Work

	Netflix has already put AI to work in some form on around 300 of its titles, Lee Sung Q, the streamer’s senior director of APAC production, said at Creative Asia, the Netflix and BIFF program for emerging talent. On the same panel, co-hosted by Netflix and the MPA, “The Outlaws” director Kang Yoon-sung put AI’s potential savings on a feature at 30% to 40% of the budget.

	Kang co-directed “Run to the West,” billed as Korea’s first feature to use AI throughout production, and made a test for “The Gulf of Aden,” a film built around military operations at sea, entirely with AI using Kling. He said the savings on that film would not come only from swapping out CG. “The shoot itself got simpler, and it cut the overall production period to some extent,” he said.

	He also said the technology often cuts out the debate and shared experience that filmmaking has relied on. “So the quality of the footage AI makes is very high, but when it comes to delivering emotion and moving audiences, I think we’re in a period where it has actually gotten worse,” Kang said.

	Lee said that when it comes to conveying emotion, a human ultimately has to touch the work once more. “I strongly agree that a human touch is absolutely essential,” he said.

	On the market floor, InnoAsia, the ACFM’s technology strand, brought in Kling, Alibaba and BytePlus. Kling teamed with filmmakers including Korean director Kim Sung-su to show how AI might reshape filmmaking, and Forum BIFF screened an AI short by Jia Zhangke. VFX veteran Hong Jae-cheol told the strand’s AI Creators Camp how images generated by AI are being slotted into production pipelines next to conventional effects, with people still steering the creative work.

	“Compared to FilMart, microdramas aren’t as big as you would expect. Same for AI. In Hong Kong they were everywhere,” Haeutle said.

	Law said AI remains very much a debate. “At the moment you’ll find that AI is in films but not in the way people are imagining it to be,” he said.
	

	Europe and Thailand Build Bridges

	By Europe! Hub’s count, 36% of the festival program was at least a European co-production. “There’s the 140 years France-Korean relationship and this year, the Italian Pavilion is very big,” Haeutle said.

	Thailand was the ACFM’s first Country of Honor, and the Busan Story Market added five Thai titles for remake. “Compared with last year, we’ve seen many more visitors coming to our booth, asking questions and showing curiosity about what Thailand has to offer,” Phakhin Chettanat, business development manager at Thailand-based Banana Sound Studio, told Variety.

	He said Asian countries are becoming more competitive, though production costs still decide where shoots go. “As talent and technical capabilities continue to improve across the region, I believe Asia will eventually become a major production hub alongside North America and Europe,” he said.

	Japan was Producer Hub’s focus country this year, with Japan’s Visual Industry Promotion Organization (VIPO) co-hosting a program that drew 188 producers from 25 countries.

title: ‘Avatar: Fire and Ash’ Composer and More Speak Out About AI at Ghent’s WSA Film Music Days: ‘We Must Continue to Defend Our Art’
description: At a recent World Soundtrack Awards industry panel, composer Simon Franglen struck a common chord when talking about his work on “Avatar: Fire and
body:
At a recent World Soundtrack Awards industry panel, composer Simon Franglen struck a common chord when talking about his work on “Avatar: Fire and Ash.”

	“We had hundreds of musicians in a room, pouring their emotion out in that precise second,” he recalled. “How can that ever be replicated by AI?”

	This year’s WSA Film Music Days, held Oct. 8–10 in Ghent, Belgium, took aim at that very question, gathering the industry for three days of talks, roundtables and mixers addressing composers’ most pressing concerns.
	

	Here are four takeaways from an event that proved composers needn’t play solo.


	Strength in Numbers 

	Labor structures are a hurdle. Unlike many other key creatives and department heads, composers in the U.S. and U.K. face legal barriers to unionizing and collective bargaining. The European Composer and Songwriter Alliance helps fill that gap, uniting national associations to lobby policymakers and guide young composers through contracts and negotiations.

	Representing more than 30,000 composers and songwriters across 57 member organizations, ECSA had a strong presence in Ghent, hosting a roundtable before receiving this year’s WSA Industry Award. 

	“There’s still a long way to go and a lot of work to do,” ECSA president Helienne Lindvall said in accepting the award. “But one thing is clear: We have become a voice to be reckoned with, giving composers and songwriters a seat at the table. Because, as someone once said, if you’re not sitting at the table, chances are you’re on the menu.” 

	Art vs. AI

	To counter the growing threat of generative AI, ECSA is also pushing to shape the EU’s evolving AI Act around three core demands: AI companies must get permission before using copyrighted music to train generative models; creators must be fairly compensated for that use; and platforms must disclose which catalogs and datasets they use. 
	

	“If we want to protect those at the heart of music creation, we must continue to defend the three fundamental principles of Authorization, Remuneration and Transparency,” Lindvall said. “In other words, our art.” 

	Platforms like AI music generator Suno make those demands all the more urgent. Lindvall had a blunt warning for musicians and composers curious about the technology. “Read the terms of service,” she implored. “Anything you upload, even if you think, ‘I’ll just upload my music and see if they can come up with a guitar lick,’ you are giving them the right to use your music and exploit it commercially, without limitation, in perpetuity.” 



	

									©Jeroen Willems
	



	Star Track: The Next Generation 

	For many panelists, AI’s short-term savings come at the expense of the next generation of composers. As music factories and generative tools take over entry-level work, newcomers risk losing a vital foothold in the industry. 

	“Hans Zimmer wouldn’t be who he is today without [getting a gig on the 1980s British game show] ‘Going for Gold,’” Franglen said. “We all start somewhere, and we all have our various steps. It’s essential that those steps exist.”

	Darrell Alexander, who runs composer agency Cool Music, sees working as an additional composer as the best entry point for anyone starting out. “It’s still better to try to be an additional composer to a master,” he said. “We accept applications for jobs, and I think that’s really important, because you can study and learn and see.” 

	Adiescar Chase is doing her part, too. After her acclaimed work on Netflix’s “Heartstopper,” she pushed to bring on additional hands for subsequent seasons. “I told production before we started, ‘Just so you know, I’m going to have an assistant this time,’” she said. “They had to trust me. I hope that in my community, the people I bring on to assist know I’m trustworthy.” 

	Looking ahead, Martin Phipps (“The Crown”) believes that creatives will always prioritize human contact — and that AI won’t eat every job.

	“It’s a skill in itself to prompt an AI,” Phipps said. “You need to employ someone to do that, and that somebody’s got to be there, for a while anyway. Though I do know a few directors who would quite like to write the music themselves, which is a worry!”
	

	Take It to the Bank 

	Beyond AI anxieties, panelists also took to the WSA to share best practices. Sound banks in particular proved well loved. 

	On Kristen Stewart’s “The Chronology of Water,” for instance, Paris Hurley skipped scoring to picture. Instead, Hurley created and collected bespoke sounds, often using her body as an instrument, then rearranged and remixed them to fit each section of the film. “This is a story that’s only told once, with a director who cares deeply about what’s being made, and it would almost be a disservice to just rock up with a collection of familiar sounds,” Hurley says. 

	“Slow Horses” composer Daniel Pemberton shares the instinct. “Creating your own sonic palette that’s unique to each project makes such a difference to a score,” he says. “So I always try to build fresh palettes. It’s like getting a new instrument each time and working out how it works. There’s a naivety to that, but also a freshness, and the material is fresher because hopefully it’s stuff people haven’t heard before.”

	Along with giving a project its own sonic identity, a sound bank can speed up the work, a real advantage on a show with a schedule as unrelenting as “Slow Horses.” 

	“The ‘Slow Horses’ sound bank took a long, long time to get working,” Pemberton says. “But now I’ve built all these sounds that are very distinctive to the show. It’s like having a synthesizer with presets that no one else has. And you can be very lazy, hold one thing down, and it still sounds cool!”

title: Serielizados Program: Steven Moffat, Ferran Adrià and Rodrigo Sorogoyen Bring Star Creator Power to Barcelona
description: Carmen Machi, Rodrigo Sorogoyen, Hagai Levi, Steven Moffat, Sue Vertue, Victoria Martín, Ferran Adrià. All will bring star power to Barcelona’s lea
body:
Carmen Machi, Rodrigo Sorogoyen, Hagai Levi, Steven Moffat, Sue Vertue, Victoria Martín, Ferran Adrià. All will bring star power to Barcelona’s leading series festival Serielizados which is set to kick-off Oct. 19 with the Catalan premiere of the 3Cat-HBO Max “In Vitro.”

	A prime launching pad for Spanish premieres, the festival will showcase six international series in competition and a four-title national competition led by the world premiere of Movistar Plus-100 Balas’ “Celeste 2,” and Catalan premiere of “Killing a Bear” (“Killing a Bear”), another Movistar Plus Original.On the industry front, Serielizados Pro will consolidate and expand its program, taking in case studies on successful co-productions, (“In Vitro,” “Segunda temporada”) trend analysis, networking sessions, and the second Mind the Gap international pitch with 11 premium projects. More than 300 delegates are expected including reps from YouTube, Mubi, RTVE, Arte France, Beta Film, ZDF, Oble, DR Sales, Imagina Sales, and many more.
	

	Betu Martínez Molero, Serielizados’ co-founder with Victor Sala, unpacks the festival’s DNA and program highlights.


	You said last year that your goal was both to up your number of visitors and to better serve the local industry. Is it mission accomplished after last year’s 80% increase in visitors and Serielizados Pro’s first Mind the Gap?

	Yes, we totally accomplished that and after growing by 80% last year, our challenge this edition is consolidation. Our main hurdle has always been convincing people to pay for a cinema ticket to watch two episodes of a series. We’ve overcome that by not only premiering great series but also bringing the talent directly to the fans.
	

	On the industry side, Serielizados Pro has settled into its identity as a boutique forum. We don’t want to be huge; we want to be effective. We focus heavily on European co-productions, matching local Catalan and Spanish creators with international agents through pitching sessions, masterclasses, and networking.

	In fact, after our first Mind the Gap Pitching, we’re already seeing participating projects secure financing and move into production, which proves that the concept works.

	This year your motto is ‘An Eye for It,’ to spotlight your unique cultural curation remit. Could you expand on this theme and why you chose it?

	When we launched Serielizados in 2013, finding great TV was almost a DIY effort. In Spain, VOD was basically limited to Canal+ and Filmin. There was very little original local production, and people were finding their favourite TV shows through obscure corners of the web. Fast forward to today, and we’ve shifted from discovery to extreme content overload. We now consume series at the same frantic pace as social media or fast food.

	That’s why our motto this year is ‘An Eye for It.’ In an era of overabundance driven by algorithms, a festival’s core job is editorial curation. We act as a filter. We spend the whole year searching for series that truly matter, offering our audience a thoughtful selection rather than an infinite scroll. We strongly believe festivals must remain trusted cultural tastemakers

	Your opening series is “In Vitro,” an HBO Max, 3Cat co-production: How important was it for you to secure this prestige show?

	It’s a festival tradition for us to open with top Catalan talent, we’ve done it with “This Is Not Sweden” and “Yo, adicto” in the past. Opening with “In Vitro” continues that legacy. It’s a powerful story with a relevant and very current topic (fertility clinics) and bringing together HBO Max and 3Cat, showing the strength of local co-productions. We’re confident “In Vitro’”will spark a strong conversation with our opening night audience and in the media.

	How was the selection process this year for the two main competitions: National and International?Every year we receive hundreds of submissions across national and international categories, this year well over 200 projects.The selection process is intense: We look for editorial coherence, distinctive voices, and strong production value. We make sure every show in competition brings something unique, avoiding generic platform filler.
	

	From the projects submitted, what trends can you identify in terms of genres, formats, creatives involved, topics, commissioners?

	This year we noticed a strong shift toward European productions, particularly from Northern and Central Europe. We think that co-production model in Europe is finally bearing fruit, delivering deeply human, socially-engaged stories connected to modern politics and everyday life. Germany was a surprise this year, the quality leap in their fiction is remarkable. Also France continues to perform at an exceptionally high level.

	Another key trend I’d point out is the crucial role of public broadcasters like Arte in France (“Etty”), ARD in Germany (“Naked,” “A Better Place”), or even Estonia’s ERR (we’ll have “In Darkness “at the online festival on Filmin), the first Estonian show ever at Serielizados.

	The feeling is that private VOD platforms often rely on safe algorithms and public networks are taking risks, backing bold, out-of-the-box auteur series like “Naked,” “A Better Place,” or “In Darkness.” For years, SVT, DR, or the BBC were the main gold standards for public TV, but now we see public broadcasters from other countries stepping up.

	Could you outline your national and international competition, and highlight one or two titles that you’re particularly eager to showcase?

	The festival motto for this year could also be “Life Through Series.” Every selected show mirrors current societal anxieties with a strong authorial voice.

	In the national competition, we’ve leaned into sophisticated dramedies and tragicomedies with a distinct Coen brothers touch (“In Vitro,” “Killing a Bear,” “Celeste S2,” “Segunda Temporada”). They explore modern human contradictions, from millennial burnout to corporate fraud and environmental hypocrisy.I’d highlight “Segunda Temporada,” from the team behind “Autodefensa,” for its sheer freshness, unique voice, and politically incorrect humor.Hosting the world premiere of “Celeste 2” is obviously a massive highlight. We premiered Season 1, which was a huge hit at the festival and later became the most-watched show of the year on Movistar Plus. Honestly, we didn’t know we needed a series about the Spanish IRS, but Diego San José absolutely nailed it. Having Carmen Machi and the creative team in Barcelona is very special. “Celeste” is the gold standard of what a dramedy should be: it balances sharp writing, great direction, and exceptional performances completely naturally.
	

	The International Competition is more eclectic, touching on everything, from sex addiction (“Naked”) to corporate eco-scandal (“Dirty Business”). Two titles I’m especially proud of are “A Better Place,” because it thinks outside the box by bringing progressive, utopian ideas about justice to a world in political crisis. Then “Ann Droid,” simply because we love Diane Morgan. Having a show created by her where she stars is fantastic. It’s a dramedy about AI with a feelgood heart, tremendous sensibility and great comedy all at the same time.



	

					Betu Martínez Molero
	



	Last year you hoped to launch a production outfit. Is it again ‘mission accomplished’ with your closing series being “Episòdic: El principi d’Arquimedes” that you’re producing?

	This is a major milestone for us, but honestly, that happened completely naturally and organically. Through initiatives like Serielizados Kick, our screenwriter talent campus, we were already nurturing new voices. All of a sudden, we realized we weren’t just discovering talent anymore, we were actually producing.

	Created alongside the Barcelona City Council and public broadcaster betevé, “Episòdic”’s purpose is to bridge the gap between film school and the professional industry, giving 38 film students from 11 educational centers their first official IMDb credit by involving them directly in the creation of a short-form TV series.

	“Episòdic “is an anthology series that adapts prestigious Catalan plays for television. Season 1 adapts Josep Maria Miró’s “El principi d’Arquimedes,” an award-winning play staged in nearly 50 countries that explores prejudice and moral panic through an innocent gesture at a swimming pool. We stepped in as executive producers, supervising the entire development and production process alongside a top professional cast.After a preview presentation at Iberseries 2026, we’re thrilled to host its world premiere as our closing session, before it’s broadcast on betevé this autumn. And we’re already working on selecting the play we’ll adapt for Season 2.

	Could you say a few words about the very special guests attending, from Rodrigo Sorogoyen, Steven Moffat, Sue Vertue, to Ferran Adrià?

	Since 2015, we’ve always aimed high, bringing creators like Dan Harmon, David Simon, Vince Gilligan and later Jesse Armstrong. Every year, we build a wishlist of our top dream guests, and Steven Moffat has always been right at the top.
	

	Having Steven in Barcelona, where “Sherlock” and “Doctor Who” have huge cult followings, is incredible. And bringing Sue Vertue completes the picture: she’s one of the U.K.’s sharpest producers, behind classics like “Mr. Bean,” which is practically part of Catalan pop culture DNA. Honestly, Rowan Atkinson is almost considered an honorary Catalan citizen!! Historically, Catalan public TV imported British comedy (“Fawlty Towers,” “The Young Ones,” “Monty Python,” “Allo Allo” etc) which deeply shaped our local comedy writers. So having Steven and Sue here is a true celebration of that cultural bridge between the U.K. and Catalonia.

	Beyond that, we always aim to create an eclectic constellation of top talent. This year we have Rodrigo Sorogoyen, arguably Spain’s finest director today, creator of the masterpiece “Antidisturbios” (“Riot Police”) and co-founder of Caballo Films, one of our favourite production companies in Spain. He’ll serve as president of our international jury during a banner year for him, fresh off “The Beloved” a world premiere at Cannes, and with a lot of international attention about his work.

	And finally, having Ferran Adrià is huge for us. Ahead of 3Cat’s premiere of “Gènesi,” the series detailing his legacy and how El Bulli revolutionized global gastronomy, Ferran will join us for an open talk at Casa Cupra. We’ll dive into “Gènesi” versus his real memories, while exploring the intersection of TV series and gastronomy. Having minds of this caliber eager to participate is the very core of what Serielizados stands for.
