title: Cynthia Erivo’s ‘Bad Fairies’ Adds Kylie Minogue, Jonathan Groff and Catherine Tate to Voice Cast
description: “Bad Fairies,” the Warner Bros. Picture Animation and Locksmith Animation musical comedy led by Cynthia Erivo, has added Kylie Minogue, Jonathan Gr
body:
“Bad Fairies,” the Warner Bros. Picture Animation and Locksmith Animation musical comedy led by Cynthia Erivo, has added Kylie Minogue, Jonathan Groff and Catherine Tate to its voice cast. 

	Minogue will voice Clowder the Cat Witch, Groff will voice Robin Goodfellow and Tate will voice the Fairy Gothmother, joining Erivo as Jayne Staplegun in the animated feature. Erivo shared the news at her Thursday evening Hollywood Bowl concert “Let Me Sing to You.”
	

	The second half of the Bowl show opened with an orchestral piece built on “Hard to Believe,” Jayne’s song from the film, which is about a group of “delightfully defiant, rule-breaking fairies.” Erivo introduced Groff and Tate, then revealed that Minogue, who was seated in the audience, would be joining the cast.


	“Bad Fairies” is set to open on May 27, 2027, and production is currently underway in London, with DNEG Animation as digital partner.

	The cast also includes Serrana Su-Ling Bliss as Fei Chang, James Acaster as Stickers and Dee Bradley Baker as Groundbeef, along with Ncuti Gatwa as Butterwort.

	Set in contemporary London, “Bad Fairies” is directed by Megan Nicole Dong and co-directed by Olivier Staphylas, from an original screenplay by Deborah Frances-White. Tony Award winners Toby Marlow and Lucy Moss (“Six: The Musical”) are writing the original songs, with a score by Isabella “Machine” Summers of Florence and the Machine.

	“’Bad Fairies’ is about characters who break the rules to do some good, and Cynthia brings that spirit to everything she does, so there was no better way to share this news than from the Hollywood Bowl stage in her voice,” said Bill Damaschke, President, Warner Bros. Pictures Animation, in a statement. “With Kylie, Jonathan and Catherine joining her, we have a cast as bold and joyful as the film itself.”
	

	“From the moment we began developing ‘Bad Fairies,’ we knew it was exactly the kind of story Locksmith exists to tell: funny, surprising and full of heart,” said Natalie Fischer, CEO of Locksmith Animation. “Cynthia Erivo’s extraordinary voice has been the soul of this film since she came on board, and we’re thrilled to have Kylie, Jonathan and Catherine bring their enormous talents to these characters. We can’t wait for audiences to meet them next May.”

	“I’m so excited to be part of ‘Bad Fairies,’ alongside the incredible Cynthia Erivo, Jonathan Groff and such a brilliant cast of voices,” said Minogue. “And getting to play both a cat and a witch? It’s a little bit magical, a little bit mischievous and a whole lot of fun.”

	“Clowder needed to be impossibly glamorous and hilariously chaotic in the same breath, and Kylie was always the dream,” said director Megan Nicole Dong. “She has made the character completely her own, and she brings this amazing energy to the booth that ends up in every frame.”

	“Jonathan finds the comedy and the heart in a character at exactly the same time, which is everything Robin Goodfellow needs, and there is no one funnier than Catherine to play our Fairy Gothmother,” said co-director Olivier Staphylas. “Our animators are building on our fabulous actors’ instincts and comic timing to create characters that feel both larger than life and genuinely real.”

	“KPop Demon Hunters” music producer Ian Eisendrath serves as executive music producer, while the film’s creative team also includes producer Carolyn Soper, editor Sim Evan-Jones, cinematographer James C.J. Williams, character designer Uwe Heidschötter, heads of story Rikke Asbjoern and Chris Garbutt, and production designers Justin Hutchinson-Chatburn and Mike Redman. Minogue is represented by Jason Weinberg at Untitled and Polly Bhowmik at Context Management. Groff is represented by Brian Boone and Joe Michota at CAA. Tate is represented by Jeremy Barber at UTA and Robert Taylor at The Artists Partnership.

description:

body:
Oct 16, 2026 12:00am PT	
	

	
		‘Norm: The Tale of Norm Macdonald’: Five Biggest Takeaways, From the ‘SNL’ Firing to Concealing His Cancer Diagnosis
	
	
			


			
			
	

									Courtesy of Netflix
	

		
	
				

	Norm Macdonald wasn’t for everyone. Armed with a deadpan delivery, devil-may-care attitude and cracker-barrel charm, the Canadian comic got his start writing for “Roseanne” before earning acclaim as the host of SNL’s Weekend Update, where his unrelenting ridicule of O.J. Simpson for being an alleged murderer — Macdonald was adamant that it wasn’t so “alleged” — eventually got him canned from the show. His one big shot at movie stardom, the Bob Saget-helmed 1998 comedy film “Dirty Work,” bombed spectacularly, and he subsequently presided over the quietly uproarious video podcast “Norm Macdonald Live” before dying from complications from leukemia in 2021 at the age of 61. Perhaps his old pal Larry King said it best, calling Macdonald, “One of the most respected comedians today, though show business has never found a place to put him.”



	In the handful of years since his death, however, Macdonald has blossomed into an internet darling, as new generations of comedy enthusiasts stumble upon his hilariously awkward late-night appearances — particularly on “Late Night with Conan O’Brien” — Weekend Update segments and podcast clips. Nobody did it like Macdonald, whose downright desiccated sense of humor is sorely absent in today’s doing-too-much comedy landscape. This new cultural appreciation for Macdonald is celebrated in “Norm: The Tale of Norm Macdonald,” a new documentary from Judd Apatow that premieres Friday on Netflix. Apatow’s loving tribute to his late pal contains no talking heads or any of the other conventions of these types of docs; rather, it explores the comedy giant’s life in Macdonald’s own words, largely borrowed from the narration of his absurdist biographical book “Based on a True Story: Not a Memoir,” as well as home videos, photos and archival interviews.

	Here are five big takeaways from “Norm: The Tale of Norm Macdonald.”


			
			
	The Weekend Update Secret Sauce
			
										
					Image Credit: ©NBC/Courtesy Everett Collection				
					
				
	Next to Chevy Chase, Macdonald is regarded as the greatest Weekend Update host in “Saturday Night Live” history. And in the documentary, he gives a lot of credit to Lori Jo Hoekstra, his longtime collaborator who produced his stand-up specials and oversaw Weekend Update during his tenure. It was Hoekstra, he says, who wanted to make their Weekend Update different from the rest of SNL by hiring a team of outside writers, including Ross Abrash and Frank Sebastiano (who joined Macdonald’s creative partner, the legendary SNL writer Jim Downey), and having its own separate comedy identity. “Lori Jo [Hoekstra] then suggested we hire outside writers so Weekend Update would have a completely different flavor from the rest of SNL,” Macdonald recalls in the doc. “We all agreed that the jokes should be stripped of any cleverness, play on words or innuendo… A joke should catch people by surprise. It should never pander. Applause is voluntary, but laughter is involuntary.”
		
			
			
	His SNL Firing by Don Ohlmeyer
			
										
					Image Credit: ©NBC/Courtesy Everett Collection				
					
				

	“If I am remembered, it will always be by the four years I spent at ‘Saturday Night Live’ — and maybe even more than that, by the events surrounding my departure from that show,” Macdonald admits in the film. And yes, the circumstances of his SNL departure have become an indispensable part of Macdonald’s lore. As the story goes, in the ‘90s, Macdonald, Downey and the Weekend Update team went hard at O.J. Simpson during his murder trial. “O.J. Simpson’s lawyers say they don’t want the families of Nicole Brown and Ronald Goldman in the courtroom during the trial. They’re afraid the presence of the family members will just remind O.J. of how much killing he still has to do,” Macdonald quipped on Update. When Simpson was acquitted of the murders, Macdonald declared on the show: “Well, it is finally official: Murder is legal in the state of California.”

	But Simpson was best friends with then-president of NBC West Coast, the late Don Ohlmeyer, who supposedly became so incensed by Macdonald’s mockery of his controversial buddy that he fired both Macdonald and Downey (Downey was later rehired in 2000) over the jokes, with Macdonald saying that Ohlmeyer called him up personally and told him he was being fired because he wasn’t funny. Ohlmeyer’s vendetta against Macdonald didn’t end there. He later tried to ban NBC from airing promos for Macdonald’s film “Dirty Work” (he lost that battle) and tried to force Conan O’Brien to stop booking Macdonald as a guest on “Late Night” (O’Brien pushed back and Ohlmeyer lost that battle, too).

		
			
			
	Concealing His Cancer Diagnosis
			
										
					Image Credit: COURTESY OF NETFLIX				
					
				

	One of Macdonald’s oldest friends, comedian Harland Williams, reveal in the film via interview clips that the comic quietly battled stomach cancer in the 1980s. In 2013, he was diagnosed with multiple myeloma and only told his family, agent and ex-wife, choosing to hide it from the public and even his closest friends. He was prescribed dexamethasone, causing him to gain considerable weight. “I was always taught that the nature of art was to conceal, not to reveal. What they do now is ‘confessional comedy,’ but when people confess things and they’re told how brave they are, because they have cancer or something and they talk about it, well, everyone has cancer. It’s not rare at all. The brave thing to do if you have cancer is to not talk about it,” Macdonald says in the doc.

	He was inspired to keep his cancer private by Richard Farnsworth, the journeyman actor who, after battling terminal cancer in secret, took his own life with a gun in October of 2000. “I remember Richard Farnsworth was an old character actor and he did a David Lynch movie called ‘The Straight Story.’ It was based on a guy who, in actual real life, drove his riding lawnmower across the state to visit his brother, who was dying. It was Richard Farnsworth’s last movie,” Macdonald explains. “He was very frail, riddled with cancer. So anyways, the point of it is, Richard Farnsworth was nominated for an Academy Award for the movie, and if he’d said he was filled with cancer, he would’ve won, for sure. But instead, he didn’t say it. In fact, no one knew it; he kept it from everyone. He didn’t want to cause people distress, so I thought, ‘Wow, how incredible to go through it alone.’”

		
			
			
	The #MeToo Movement
			
										
					Image Credit: Getty Images				
					
				
	Like many comedians of his era, Macdonald did not have a spotless track record, and the uproar over his comments about the #MeToo movement are briefly explored in the doc. On Sept. 18, 2021, Macdonald conducted an interview with The Hollywood Reporter where he defended pals Louis C.K. and Roseanne, and admitted he was grateful that the #MeToo movement had “slowed down a little bit,” adding, “There are very few people that have gone through what they have, losing everything in a day. Of course, people will go, ‘What about the victims?’ But you know what? The victims didn’t have to go through that.” (He later apologized on Twitter.) Macdonald, who was promoting his David Letterman-produced Netflix talk show “Norm Macdonald Has a Show,” subsequently had his “Tonight Show” appearance canceled and received considerable backlash online and in the media. Two weeks after his much-derided comments, The Daily Beast published a report detailing Macdonald’s alleged history of sexual harassment and the measures comedy clubs needed to take to protect women from him, which is absent from the doc.
		
			
			
	On Death
			
										
					Image Credit: Netflix				
					
				
	One of Macdonald’s quotes that really stuck with me from “Norm: The Tale of Norm Macdonald” dealt with death — something the comedian stared directly in the face over the final years of his life while battling cancer. “Death is a funny thing — not funny ha-ha like a Woody Allen movie, but funny-strange like a Woody Allen marriage. When it’s unexpected, death comes fast like a ravenous wolf; when it’s expected, it comes slow and patient like a snake,” he offers. “The doctor tells you how far away it is, and when exactly it will be at your door, and when it will be at the foot of your bed, and when it will be on your flesh. It’s all right there on their clipboards… I have a theory that people are in deep denial about death, and I’m not.”
		
	
	


	
		More from Variety

            Music icon Billy Joel is giving a rare update on his health and he sadly says he may never perform again. 
      
    
            In an interview with The Hollywood Reporter the “Just The Way You Are” singer said when it comes to his future as a performer … “I don’t know. I have to take a series of tests before I know, but … I’m not allowed to drive. And I can’t do performances because what the neurologist told me, every time you do a show, it’s like you’re getting a concussion.”
      
    
            As we told you, Billy is currently auctioning off over 70 of his motorcycles and told The Hollywood Reporter “I have a condition called hydrocephalus, which makes driving a little bit iffy. So I realized it’s time for me to turn it over to somebody else.”
      
    
            Proceeds from the sale of Billy's bikes will go toward his organization, The Joel Foundation.
      

            Despite his positive attitude towards his diagnosis, Billy hasn’t had the best of luck recently. Just last month, Joel lost his best friend and former bandmate Jon Small and gave a moving tribute to Small on his Instagram, saying “Losing Jon has hit me in a way I have never experienced. It is difficult to imagine this world without him in it.” 
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            The good news is Joel said his memory and balance improved after his surgery, and continued ... “I’m not going anywhere, I’m here. I’m still here.”

'Training Day' Charlotte Ayanna
                          Arrested for Allegedly Kicking Cop, Spreading Human Ashes
                      
                  
                                                                        Published 
                              October 16, 2026
                            12:00 AM PDT
                                                                            
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            Charlotte Ayanna, the actress who played Ethan Hawke's wife in "Training Day," was arrested in West Hollywood after allegedly kicking a deputy and spreading cremated human remains in a home ... TMZ has learned.
      
    
            Law enforcement sources tell TMZ ... deputies were responding to a call for a welfare check on October 8 when they say the situation took a violent turn.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            According to cops, the alleged victim told deputies Ayanna -- born Charlotte Lopez -- threatened his life, battered him, and spread cremated human remains inside the residence.
      

            Authorities also allege Ayanna kicked a deputy during the investigation ... and she was ultimately arrested on suspicion of criminal threats, elder abuse, battery on a peace officer, and depositing human remains outside of a cemetery.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            On Monday, prosecutors filed three misdemeanor counts ... battery, elder or dependent adult abuse, and battery on a peace officer.
      
    
            When contacted for comment, Ayanna told TMZ, "It was an unfair illegal false arrest. Not only was I never read my rights, including the Miranda rights, but | was never even interviewed to talk to.”
      
    
            Ayanna is known for her role in "Training Day," which starred Denzel Washington, and "Love the Hard Way" with Adrien Brody. She won the Miss Teen USA competition in 1993.
      
    
            She's being held on $50,000 bail.
